C4.3.14 Code Enforcement
Code enforcement in the city of Dos Palos is generally handled by the Dos Palos Police Department.
The City currently has one Code Enforcement officer, who is completing training to become an
official police officer, where general safety and welfare is prioritized over conducting active
investigations. Code enforcement is typically complaint based. Hazardous building conditions are



2024-2032 Housing Element                                                                       C4-29
Merced County Association of Governments
Merced County Multi-Jurisdictional Housing Element (2024-2032)

referred to the Building Official, who then notifies the City’s building inspectors. The City contracts
with CSG Consultants to conduct building inspections.
The City has the power to inspect and declare unsafe any structure or piece of equipment, be it
existing or under construction, that does not meet specific Municipal Code standards. These include,
but are not limited to, structures with insufficient modes of egress; structures that are unsafe or
that have been made structurally unsound due to fire, earthquake, or other natural disaster;
buildings that are deemed a public nuisance; and buildings that have been constructed or
maintained in violation of local or state law. Once a building has been declared unsafe, the building
official may issue notice that the structure be repaired, vacated, or demolished within a reasonable
amount of time and with the appropriate permits.
The enforcement of building codes in the city is centered on the inspection of new construction and
remodels or renovations requiring building permits. However, for existing structures, City staff
prioritize code enforcement complaints according to the severity of the violation on the community
and individuals. Situations that appear to pose a serious risk to health and safety are given top
priority; others are pursued in the order in which they are received, as resources are available. In
most cases for non-emergency complaints, a warning letter or courtesy notice is sent to the alleged
violator to verify the status of the potential compliant and to obtain compliance.

C4.3.14.1 Conclusion
The City contracts building inspections to a qualified consultant, but main enforcement activities are
handled by law enforcement. Code enforcement being conducted by law enforcement could result
in low-income families not reporting housing conditions for fear of displacement if they are not able
to afford repairs needed to address code enforcement violations. The City has not adopted the most
recent (2022) California Building Code. This is a constraint to housing.

C4.3.14.2 Recommended Action
The City will implement Housing Program 6 to adopt the most recent (2022) California Building
Code. As part of Program 16, the City will identify a code enforcement specialist on staff to provide
technical assistance and information to property owners of lower income units to address code
enforcement issues separate from law enforcement.

C4.4 Environmental Constraints
A community’s environmental setting affects the feasibility and cost of developing housing.
Environmental issues range from the availability of water to the suitability of land for development
due to potential exposure to seismic, flooding, wildfire, and other hazards. If not properly
recognized and accommodated in residential design, these environmental features could potentially
endanger lives and property. This section summarizes environmental constraints to housing
development in Dos Palos.

C4.4.1 Flood
Merced County has a number of surface water resources including rivers, creeks, reservoirs, and
canals. These resources include three rivers (Merced, San Joaquin, and Chowchilla), seven major
creeks (Quinto, Romero, Bear, Los Banos, Owens, Mariposa, and Deadman), five reservoirs (San Luis,




C4-30
                                                                                                            City of Dos Palos
                                                                                                  Housing Constraints Analysis

O’Neil Forebay, Los Banos Creek, and Burns), and four major canals (Delta-Mendota, San Luis, the
California Aqueduct, and Eastside).
Flood is a natural occurrence in the Central San Joaquin Valley. The Valley is a natural drainage basin
for thousands of acres of foothill and mountain land of the Sierras. Approximately 750,000 acres in
the San Joaquin Subbasin are prone to flooding. In Merced County, the flood plains of the San
Joaquin and Merced rivers and their tributaries encompass nearly one half of the Valley floor.
Merced County has an area of roughly 380,010 acres of land that is subject to 100-year frequency
floods. However, the city of Dos Palos is not located within the San Joaquin Valley floodplain.
Flood zone mapping by the Federal Emergency Management Authority (FEMA) indicates that no
area of the City is located within the 100-year floodplain. According to the Merced County Local
Hazard Mitigation Plan, the City is at low risk of flood and levee failure.

C4.4.2 Seismic Zones
The nearest faults of major significance to Dos Palos are the San Andreas to the west, approximately
15 miles from the county line; the Hayward and Calaveras faults to the northwest; the White Wolf,
Garlock, and Sierra Nevada faults to the south; and the Bear Mountain Fault Zone about five miles
east of and parallel to the eastern border of Merced County. These faults have been and will
continue to be the principal source of seismic activity affecting the County of Merced, including the
City of Dos Palos. The only fault known inside the County is the “Ortigalita,” also known as the
“Telsa-Ortigalita Fault,” located in the western quarter of the County, dissecting the Coast Range in
a northwesterly direction. This fault has not been historically active. There have been no records of
major seismic activity originating in the county, with most epicenters in the county being below a
magnitude 4.0. There are no Alquist Priolo Earthquake Fault Zones in Dos Palos. According to the
Merced County Multi-Jurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan, the city of Dos Palos is subject to
occasional earthquakes of critical severity.3

C4.4.3 Wildland/Urban Fire Hazards
Fire hazard potential is largely dependent on the extent and type of vegetation, known as surface
fuels, that exists within a region. Fire hazards are typically highest in heavily wooded, undeveloped
areas as trees are a greater source of fuel than low-lying brush or grassland. Suburban, urban areas,
or rocky barren areas have minimal surface fuels and therefore typically have the lowest fire hazard.
The California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE) ranks fire hazard of wildland
areas of the state using four main criteria: fuels, weather, assets at risk, and level of service. CAL
FIRE has mapped moderate and High Fire Hazard Severity Zones (FHSZ) in Merced County, outside
the city boundaries. 4 While there are no fire severity zones within the city boundaries, the city is
designated as being at increased risk from wildfires5

There are few environmental constraints on future development of lands for housing in the Dos

the vicinity, including wetland areas or other significant areas of protected habitat. While there is a
moderate risk of earthquake damage in the city, and future wildfire occurrences are likely. The City
requires all new development and subdivisions to comply with California Fire and Building Code
requirements for health and safety. As a result, there are no significant environmental constraints to
housing development.

C5         Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing

C5.1 Introduction
This section of the Housing Element analyzes issues relating to fair housing for the City of Dos Palos.
This analysis is based on the directives from State Assembly Bill (AB) 686. Background information
on AB 686, countywide fair housing services, data sources, and analysis of the regional Affirmatively
Furthering Fair Housing (AFFH) issues are included in Chapter 5, Regional Assessment of Fair
Housing.

C5.2 Methodology
This AFFH analysis evaluates fair housing issues on the following topics:
   Fair Housing Enforcement and Outreach Capacity
   Integration and Segregation Patterns and Trends
   Racially and Ethnically Concentrated Areas of Poverty
   Disparities in Access to Opportunity
   Disproportionate Housing Needs
   Other Relevant Factors, including limited English proficiency, farmworker housing needs, and
    housing stock type
   Analysis of Housing Sites Inventory using AFFH indicators
   Local Area Knowledge, which includes a discussion of historic land use and segregation patterns
    and input from sources of local knowledge, including advocates for people with special needs,
    housing development and advocacy organizations, housing and social services providers, and
    low-income residents

This analysis identifies patterns and trends at the local scale. Where appropriate, the analysis refers
to the regional AFFH analysis provided in Chapter 5, Regional Assessment of Fair Housing, which
analyzes patterns and trends of the county and Northern San Joaquin Valley (SJV) Subregion
comprised of San Joaquin, Stanislaus, and Merced Counties.
For the purposes of this analysis, the city is divided into four neighborhoods: North Dos Palos, East
Dos Palos, South Dos Palos, and West Dos Palos (Figure C5-1). These neighborhoods were based on
Census block group delineations and are discussed further in Chapter C6, Housing Resources. Most
of the geographic analysis of fair housing issues in Dos Palos is based on the California Department
of Housing and Community Development (HCD) AFFH Data Viewer described in Chapter 5, Regional
Assessment of Fair Housing. The AFFH Data Viewer relies on information provided by the Census
and other data sources at the census tract and block group level. West Dos Palos is comprised of
open land and contains very few (if any) residential units. As a result, it is not included in this
analysis.

Dos Palos is made up of three census tracts with some tracts spanning areas outside of the city

   North Dos Palos: Consists of one census tract, Census Tract 24.02, and is comprised of the

C5.3 Data Sources
To conduct this analysis, the City utilized data from a variety of sources discussed in Chapter 5,
Regional Assessment of Fair Housing. Additionally, the analysis includes a discussion of historic land
use and segregation patterns and input from sources of local knowledge, including advocates for
people with special needs, housing development and advocacy organizations, housing and social
services providers, and low-income residents.

C5.4 Summary of AFFH Analysis Findings
The city of Dos Palos is predominantly Hispanic/Latino. The percentage of non-white population is
lower than that of Merced County and the median incomes are slightly lower than observed in the
county. The City has high rates of poverty, low median household incomes, and a moderate
percentage of low- and moderate-income (LMI) residents. Large portions of the city mostly consist
of areas considered low-resource and high poverty and segregation. The prevalence of low-resource
areas in these neighborhoods is a result of lack of access to transit, lack of economic opportunities
such as access to jobs, restrictive zoning and land use patterns, high pollution burden, and high
social vulnerability of residents. There is very limited transit within the city, as well as high pollution
burden. A large percentage of renters in Dos Palos are experiencing housing cost burden (spending
more than 30 percent of household income on housing costs), but residents in the city are at low
risk of displacement. South Dos Palos has a higher concentration of LMI residents than other areas
of the city, and North Dos Palos has a higher concentration of non-white residents. North Dos Palos
and South Dos Palos have higher median incomes than the rest of the city. Below is a summary of
AFFH analysis findings by neighborhood in Dos Palos.

C5.5 Fair Housing Resources
Enforcement and Outreach Capacity
The City of Dos Palos refers fair housing inquiries to Central California Legal Services (CCLS), a
nonprofit organization, that provides fair housing information and resources to residents and
housing providers. The CCLS helps tenants in disputes with their landlords and bring cases to ensure
local governments follow the law to provide low-income housing. They also refer individuals who
are facing housing voucher discrimination to resources. Organizations providing fair housing services
throughout the county are discussed in Chapter 5, Regional Assessment of Fair Housing. There are
no active or recent fair housing lawsuits, settlements, or legal cases in Dos Palos.

C5.6 Compliance with Fair Housing Laws
C5.6.1 Fair Housing Laws
In an effort to end housing segregation, the United States Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of
1968, making housing discrimination based on race, color, national origin, or religion illegal. In 1974,
Congress amended the Fair Housing Act to include sex as a protected category. Then in 1988,
Congress again amended the Fair Housing Act by passing the Fair Housing Amendments Act, making
housing discrimination against families with children and people with disabilities unlawful. The Fair



C5-4
                                                                                          City of Dos Palos
                                                              Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing (AFFH)

Housing Amendments Act also incorporated accessibility standards for new multi-family units and
“reasonable accommodations” for people with disabilities into the Fair Housing Act.
In addition to prohibiting discrimination based on federal laws, the State of California has enacted a
number of statutes that mirror and, in certain cases, extend federal fair housing protections. The
Unruh Civil Rights Act of 1959 and subsequent court decisions require equal access to the
accommodations, advantages, facilities, privileges, or services of all business establishments
regardless of protected status. The courts have interpreted this Act to prohibit any arbitrary
discrimination based in any class distinction, regardless of whether or not that basis is enumerated
in the Act.
The Fair Employment and Housing Act of 1963 is the primary state law that prohibits discrimination
in the sale, rental, lease negotiation, or financing of housing based on race, color, religion, sex,
marital status, national origin, and ancestry. The California Fair Housing Act of 1992 brought state
laws into conformity with the Federal Fair Housing Act of 1988 and added protections for people
with a “mental and physical disability” and “familial status.” The Act also requires that housing
providers allow persons with disabilities to modify their premises to meet their needs.
The Ralph Civil Rights Act of 1976 provides that all persons have the right to be free from any
violence, or intimidation by threat of violence, committed against their persons or property because
of their race, color, religion, ancestry, national origin, political affiliation, sexual orientation, sex,
age, disability, or position in a labor dispute. The Act prohibits violence or threat of the same in
rental housing situations. The Banes Civil Rights Act also forbids interference by force or threat with
an individual's constitutional or statutory rights in places of worship, housing, and private property.
The federal protected classes include:
   Color
   Disability
   Familial status
   National origin
   Race
   Religion
   Sex

The additional State of California protected classes include:
   Age
   Ancestry
   Arbitrary discrimination
   Gender
   Gender identity
   Gender expression
   Genetic information
   Marital status
   Sexual orientation
   Source of income



2024-2032 Housing Element                                                                             C5-5
Merced County Association of Governments
Merced County Multi-Jurisdictional Housing Element (2024-2032)

The City of Dos Palos strives to offer equal access to the housing opportunities for all. The City’s
Housing Element includes Goals, Policies, and Programs that facilitate and promote affirmatively
furthering fair housing, including:
   Goal 7: Promote housing opportunities and access for residents regardless of age, race, religion,
    sex, marital status, ancestry, national origin, color, disability, or economic level in compliance
    with local, state, and federal fair housing laws.
     Policy 7.1: Promote meaningful and informed participation of residents, community groups,
        and governmental agencies in all local housing and community development activities.
     Policy 7.2: Comply with federal, state, and local fair housing anti-discrimination laws
        ensuring equal access to housing regardless of circumstances as protected by fair housing
        laws.
     Policy 7.3: Provide fair housing services to city residents and ensure that residents are
        aware of their fair housing rights.
     Policy 7.4: Provide residents with housing mobility options by facilitating the development
        of a variety of housing types and expanding access to housing services.
     Policy 7.5: Protect tenants from discriminatory housing practices and displacement.
     Policy 7.6: Promote the integration of affordable and special needs housing in existing and
        planned neighborhoods.

The City of Dos Palos is also taking meaningful actions to ensure compliance with SB 329 and SB 222,
expanding the source of income protection to include “federal, state, or local public assistance and
federal, state, or local housing subsidies.” Prior to these bills, the source of income protection
excluded public housing subsidies, such as the Housing Choice Vouchers (HCVs), in the definition of
income. Both bills went into effect on January 1, 2020. As stated in the AFFH Meaningful Actions
Matrix in Chapter C7, Housing Plan, the City will work to develop informational materials to expand
outreach and education on SB 329 and SB 229 to promote the use and expand locational choices for
Housing Choice Vouchers.
The City of Dos Palos complies with the following state and federal fair housing laws:
   Fair Housing Act; Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 – the City complies by ensuring its
    actions related to housing are not discriminatory through City protocols, decision-making
    procedures, and adhering to non-discrimination requirements of federal funding programs.
   Rehabilitation Act of 1973 – see Fair Housing Act; also, the City complies through its accessibility
    protocols.
   American Disabilities Act – the City complies with ADA through building permit review and
    issuance and as described in Chapter C4, Housing Constraints Analysis, under the heading
    Housing for Persons with Disabilities).
   California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) and FEHA Regulations – the City complies
    through established City protocols for hiring and decision making, mandatory trainings for City
    staff, and legal counsel and advisement.
   Government Code Section 65008 – the City ensures that the City’s actions are not discriminatory
    through training programs conducted by the City’s Human Resources Department. Programs are
    included in this Housing Element to facilitate housing for all households, including protected
    classes (e.g., programs regarding residential care facilities, reasonable accommodation, and
    emergency shelters), including Program 8 Facilitating Affordable Housing Development.

   Government Code Section 8899.50 – Chapter G5 of this Housing Element documents
    compliance with Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing requirements.
   Government Code Section 11135 et. seq. – the City complies with anti-discrimination

    the areas planned for development. The City increased the Sphere of Influence during the
    previous General Plan update in 2012 to encompass a total of 33,463 acres. Therefore, there are
    no limits on growth control that would discourage housing development in the city.

C5.7 Ability to Address Complaints
The California Civil Rights Department (CRD), formerly the Department of Fair Employment and
Housing (DFEH), maintains a record of housing discrimination complaints filed in local jurisdictions.
United States (U.S.) Department of Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD’s) Office of Fair
Housing and Equal Opportunity (FHEO) also collects fair housing complaint data. Fair housing
complaints may be filed with either the CRD or FHEO, however, the FHEO may refer complaints to
the state or local agency for investigation. According to the AFFH Data Viewer, between 2013 and
2022, a total of three fair housing inquiries were filed with the FHEO in Dos Palos. No basis for the
inquiries is provided.

C5.8 Segregation and Integration Patterns and Trends
Race and Ethnicity
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, Hispanic/Latino residents comprise the largest racial/ethnic
group in Dos Palos (approximately 70 percent). South Dos Palos is the most diverse area of the city,
containing populations with at least 60 to 80 percent non-white residents (Figure C5-2).
Comparatively, the rest of the city is comprised of at least 40 to 60 percent non-white residents.
This is similar to the rest of the western part of Merced County, but lower than certain areas of

percent of the population are non-white.
From 2011 to 2021, the racial/ethnic diversity in Dos Palos increased. The percent of white residents
decreased 10 percent between 2011 and 2021, while the percent of Hispanic/Latino residents
increased by four percent. Asian American/Pacific Islander increased from zero to approximately 11
percent, and other/multiple races increased by approximately six percent. Black/African American
residents decreased slightly (Table C5-1). Hispanic/Latino residents remained the largest
racial/ethnic group in the city, equaling approximately two-thirds of the total population in 2021.
This is higher than the region, where approximately Hispanic/Latino residents made up 47 percent
of the population.

Familial Status
Familial status refers to the presence of children under the age of 18 and the martial status of the
head of the household. Families with children may face housing discrimination by landlords who
fear that children will cause property damage. Examples of differential treatment include limiting
the number of children in an apartment complex or confining households with children to a specific
location. These actions are potentially discriminatory. Single-parent households are protected by
fair housing law.
Dos Palos has a lower percentage of households with children compared to Merced County and the
Northern SJV region. Dos Palos has a total of 1,661 households in 2021. Households with children
present comprised approximately 29 percent (486 households) of the total households in Merced
County. This is less than the region, where 37 percent of households have children present.
Married-couple families with children comprised the largest share of households with children (56
percent), which is higher than the county (49 percent). Most single-parent households are female-
headed, single-parent households (24 percent). As shown in Table C5-3, single-parent, female-
headed households are more likely to rent than own, comprising approximately 16 percent of
renter-occupied households but only one percent of owner-occupied households.

Household Income
Household income is directly connected to the ability to afford housing. Higher-income households
are more likely to own rather than rent housing. As household income decreases, households tend
to pay a disproportionate amount of their income for housing and the number of persons occupying
unsound and overcrowded housing increases. To achieve fair housing objectives, people in low-
income households must have choice in housing opportunities—that is, when they are able to
locate units that are affordable and well maintained in all parts of a jurisdiction and region.
This section identifies household income disparities using data based on median household income
and low- or moderate-income (LMI) geographies. HUD defines an LMI area as a census tract or block
group where over 51 percent of the population is LMI. The definition of LMI is based on HUD income
definitions of up to 80 percent of the area median income (AMI). Data for this analysis is from the
HUD Low- and Moderate-Income Summary based on the 2017-2021 American Community Survey
(most recent available data).1
As of 2021 (most recent available data), Dos Palos has a median household income of $60,250 per
year, more than the county’s median income of $53,992 but significantly lower than the state
median household income of $87,100. As shown in Figure C5-11, median household income in the
city is highest in North Dos Palos and South Dos Palos. The census tract that encompasses these
neighborhoods has a median income of $62,004. East Dos Palos has a median income of $31,976.
This census tract is mostly made up of unincorporated Merced County, which may interfere with the
median income in these areas. However, the majority of residential units in this census tract are
located within the boundaries of Dos Palos.
LMI populations are prevalent throughout the western part of Merced County and the city of Dos
Palos (Figure C5-12). North Dos Palos has the highest percentage of LMI residents (71 percent),
followed by East Dos Palos (53 percent). South Dos Palos has the lowest percentage of LMI residents
(45 percent).

Racially and Ethnically Concentrated Areas of Poverty
To identify racially and ethnically concentrated areas of poverty (known as R/ECAPs), the California
Tax Credit Allocation Committee (TCAC) includes a poverty concentration and racial segregation
filter that aligns with HUD’s R/ECAP methodology but is intended to reflect the level of racial and
ethnic diversity more effectively. TCAC categorizes census tracts that have both a poverty rate of
over 30 percent and that are designated as being racially segregated (overrepresentation of people
of color relative to the region) as areas of high segregation and poverty.
In city of Dos Palos, there are no designated areas of high segregation and poverty. While no areas
of Dos Palos are designated, East Dos Palos has a high percent of LMI residents, low median income,
and a non-white population of 59 percent. Areas of high segregation and poverty in the Northern
SJV region are found in larger cities. This includes the cities of Lodi, Stockton, Modesto, Turlock,
Merced, and Los Banos.

Poverty and Segregation
Approximately 11 percent of the population in Dos Palos are living below the poverty line, which is
13 percent lower than the county (24 percent). Poverty rates are evenly distributed throughout Dos
Palos. In all census tracts, between 10 and 20 percent of the population falls below the poverty line
(Figure C5-13). This is similar to the majority of the rest of Merced County, but less than other
nearby jurisdictions, such as Livingston and Merced, which contain areas where over 40 percent of
the population live below the poverty line.

Concentrated Areas of Affluence
HCD’s AFFH Data Viewer identifies Racially Concentrated Areas of Affluence (RCAAs), defined as
white, affluent communities as census tracts that have a white population that is 1.25 times higher
than Merced County and a household median income 1.5 times higher than the AMI. There are no
RCAAs in Dos Palos. North and South Dos Palos have incomes that exceed the county’s household
median income of $53,992 per year. However, these neighborhoods also have high percentages of
non-white residents. Within the region, RCAAs are located primarily in areas surrounding larger
cities such as Merced, Atwater, and Los Banos.

Subsidized Housing
According to the California Housing Partnership, there are no affordable housing buildings in Dos
Palos, but there is one affordable housing buildingproject located just outside the city’s boundaries
located east of State Route 33, south of Valeria Street, and west of Carol Avenue. The Dos Palos
Apartments complex, built in 1989, contains 78 affordable units.
The HACM administers HCVs in Dos Palos. According to the AFFH Data Viewer, there are 75
households (8.41 percent of the renter population) that receive rental assistance through HCVs
within Dos Palos and the surrounding unincorporated county. The geography used by HUD to
measure HCV program participants includes a significant portion of unincorporated county land.
However, the majority of housing units are located in the incorporated city (Figure C5-14).

Conclusion
Dos Palos is predominantly Hispanic/Latino, with 67 percent of its population identifying as
Hispanic/Latino. Hispanic/Latino residents are the predominant population throughout the city.East
Dos Palos faces more challenges than the other areas of the city, including the highest percentage of
disabled residents (10 to 20 percent), highest percentage of female-headed households (73 percent
of households), a high percent of LMI residents, and lowest median income in the city. Most of the
cCity’s multi-family developments are located in East Dos Palos and a significant portion of East Dos
Palos housing stock is more than 30 years old.

C5.9 Disparities in Access to Opportunities
Transit Access and Walkability
There is limited transit within Dos Palos. “The Bus,” Merced County’s Regional Transit System, was
formed from the consolidation of four former local public transit service providers in July 1996.
Today The Bus is the single public transportation service provider for all of Merced County. The Bus
operates 15 fixed routes throughout the region. The Bus offers veterans, seniors and Americans
with Disabilities Act (ADA)-eligible passengers to ride for free on all services provided by The Bus
throughout Merced County. No bus routes travel through Dos Palos, but The Bus offers other transit
services in Dos Palos. In addition, the Los Banos Commuter is a fixed route bus service stops in Dos
Palos Y and connects to Los Banos, El Nido, and the city of Merced.
The Bus offers the following services in Dos Palos:
      Paratransit is a curb-to-curb shred transit service for persons with a disability and seniors.
       Paratransit service is available in every city and community in Merced County and operates
       between 6:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., Monday through Friday and 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. on Saturday
       and Sunday.
      The Micro Bus is a shared, on-demand transit service that stops at designed stops throughout
       Dos Palos and other communities in western Merced County that offers curb-to-curb service
       and reduced rates for seniors and persons with disabilities. Seniors, veterans and Americans
       with Disability Act eligible passengers can ride for free.

AllTransit is an online database that examines factors related to transit access and produces a
performance score that reveals the social and economic impact of transit, such as connectivity and
access to jobs. Dos Palos received an average AllTransit performance score of 1.2 which equates to a
very low combination of trips per week and number of jobs accessible enabling a negligible number
of people to take transit to work.2 This score is lower than scores for larger cities in the region, such
as Merced (4.7) and Atwater (3.2).
Walk Score is a private company that offers a walkability index on its website which measures the
pedestrian friendliness of a given location by analyzing walking routes to nearby amenities and
examining population density and road metrics, including block length and intersection density. 3 The
most walkable areas in Dos Palos are North Dos Palos and South Dos Palos, which received a walk

    AllTransit.Org, 2021. https://alltransit.cnt.org/
3

                                                                                Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing (AFFH)

score of 61 and 64 out of 100. This is considered “somewhat walkable.” East Dos Palos received a
walk score of 33, which is considered “car dependent.”
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) publishes the National Walkability Index that ranks
block groups based on factors such as street intersection density, proximity to transit stops, and
diversity of land uses, which are chosen for their ease of measurement and understanding, and each
block group is ranked and assigned a score based on these variables.4 According to the National
Walkability Index, North Dos Palos and South Dos Palos are considered above average walkable
(Figure C5-15). East Dos Palos is considered below average walkable and West Dos Palos is the least
walkable.
The City is actively working on efforts to improve pedestrian and bicycle safety. The City
implemented bike lanes along Center Avenue in the eastern portion of the city and is exploring
adding the addition of bike lanes along Blossom Street. Several sidewalks are in need of repair to
promote pedestrian safety. The City is currently participating in a Local Road Safety Plan along with
other jurisdictions in the County in collaboration with the Merced Council Association of
Governments (MCAG).

Access to Quality Education
Educational outcomes are measured through the educational opportunity index, which measures
the percentage of fourth-grade students testing proficient in reading and math within three miles of
a census block group. Scores range from 0 to 1, with 1 being the most positive educational outcome,
and 0 being the least positive educational outcome. Educational outcomes are low to moderate
across Dos Palos (Figure C5-16). This is similar to the rest of western Merced County, but lower than
most jurisdictions in eastern Merced County, such as Livingston and Atwater.
Dos Palos is served by the Dos Palos-Oro Loma Joint Unified School District (DPOLJUSD). DPOLJUSD
serves a population base of approximately 5,000 and employs approximately 121 teachers.
DPOLJUSD operates six schools within the district, including one preschool, two elementary schools,
one middle school, one high school, and one alternative education school. According to Ed-Data,
DPOLJUSD has an overall graduation rate of 91 percent. Approximately 24 percent of students who
are classified as English learners, and 86 percent are eligible for free or reduce priced meals. 5
The DPOLJUSD middle school is located approximately one mile outside east of the city to the east
limits. DPOLJUSD provides buses to the school, but due to the rural nature of the community, bus
rides for students can take up to an hour each way.

Economic Outcomes
TCAC measures economic opportunity by census tract. They consider poverty, adult education,
employment, job proximity, and median home values. A higher economic index score reflects more
positive economic outcomes. Economic outcomes are low across Dos Palos. Across the city,
economic scores between zero and 0.17 (out of 1) are recorded. This is lower than much of the rest
of Merced County, particularly the northeastern portion of the county, which has an economic
opportunity score between 0.8 and 1 (Figure C5-17).

According to ACS estimates, Dos Palos has an employment rate of 50 percent of persons 16 years
and over, which is slightly higher than the employment rate for the county (49 percent). The 2017-
2021 ACS estimates show that the average salary in Dos Palos in 2021 was $60,250. The largest
industries in Dos Palos are agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, and mining (21 percent of
employed population); educational services, health care, and social assistance (13 percent); and
construction (13 percent). Educational services, health care, and social assistance and agriculture,
forestry, fishing and hunting, and mining are also the largest industries in the county based on
employment.
According to Merced County, Foster Poultry Farms in Livingston, UC Merced in Merced, Mercy
Medical Center in Merced, and Hilmar Cheese in Hilmar are the largest employers in Merced
County, within commuting distance of Dos Palos. Industrial and commercial zones are concentrated
in North Dos Palos.

Healthy and Safe Housing Environment
The CalEnviroScreen map for Dos Palos identifies the degree to which communities are considered
burdened by pollution. Pollution burden is high throughout Dos Palos. The majority of the city has
an environmental score of approximately 80, out of 100 (with 100 being the highest pollution
burden). This is similar to the majority of the rest of the county. The western tip of West Dos Palos,
which contains very few residential units, has an environmental score of 92. (Figure C5-18).
Throughout the City, the biggest sources of pollution are ozone, pesticides, and lead paint in
housing. The TCAC environmental opportunity map also identifies pollution burden, using
CalEnviroScreen scores. However, unlike CalEnviroScreen, the TCAC map compares census tracts to
other census tracts within the same council of governments to show differences in pollution burden
within the region. According to the TCAC opportunity map, environmental outcome scores range
between 0.8 and 1.0, with 1.0 being the more positive score, in North Dos Palos, South Dos Palos,
and East Dos Palos. The western tip of West Dos Palos has slightly lower environmental scores of 0.6
to 0.8 (Figure C5-19).
Senate Bill (SB) 535 tasks the California Environmental Protection Agency with identifying
disadvantaged communities. Disadvantaged communities are low-income areas that are
disproportionately affected by environmental pollution and other hazards. Under SB 535, a
minimum of 25 percent of funds from the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, funded by revenue from
the state’s cap-and-trade emissions program, goes to projects that benefit disadvantaged
communities. All of Dos Palos is considered a disadvantaged community under SB 535
(Figure C5-20). This is due to the fact that population characteristics such as asthma, linguistic
isolation, poverty, unemployment, and others were high throughout the city and the western
portion of the county, in addition to the pollution burden described above.

C5.10 Disproportionate Housing Needs
Disproportionate housing needs refers to a condition in which there are significant disparities in the
proportion of members of a protected class experiencing a category of housing need, or the total
population experiencing that category of housing need in the applicable geographic area. To analyze
the extent of disproportionate housing needs, this section reviews HUD Comprehensive Housing
Affordability Strategy (CHAS) data on housing cost burden, overcrowding, and substandard housing
conditions (collectively known as “housing problems”); homelessness; and displacement risk.

Housing Problems
According to federal law, “housing problems” refers to any of four housing issues: cost burden and
severe cost burden, overcrowding, and substandard housing conditions.
Approximately 35 percent of total households in Dos Palos experienced housing problems. About 16
percent of total households experienced severe housing problems. This is lower than the region,
where 41 percent of total households experienced housing problems and 23 percent of households
experienced severe housing problems.

Substandard Housing Conditions
A housing unit is considered substandard if it lacks complete plumbing or kitchen facilities.
According to 2017-2021 ACS estimates, all units within the Dos Palos have complete plumbing and
kitchen facilities.
Approximately 69 percent of Dos Palos’ housing stock was constructed prior to 1980 and is
therefore more than 40 years old. These units may need repair and modernization improvements. In
particular, due to the age of the housing stock in East Dos Palos, rehabilitation and replacement
needs are greatest in this area. The newer developments in the city have occurred in the north and
south areas. Two new subdivisions in these areas have slightly larger lots (around 6,000 square feet)
and are different architecturally from the older homes.

Housing Cost Burden
The rate of cost burden (spending more than 30 percent of household income on housing costs) is
high throughout Dos Palos. Cost burden by homeowners ranges between 20 and 40 percent of
owner-occupied households across the city (Figure C5-21). This is lower than other nearby
jurisdictions, such as Atwater and Merced, which have areas where 60 to 80 percent of owners are
cost burdened. Cost burden among homeowners is higher than among renters within the region,
with 56 percent of homeowners experiencing cost burden.
For renter households, cost burden is highest in East Dos Palos, where between 40 and 60 percent
of the renter population are cost burdened (Figure C5-22). In North Dos Palos and South Dos Palos,
20 to 40 percent of renters are cost burdened. Similar to owner-occupied households, this is lower
than other nearby jurisdictions such as Atwater and Merced, which have areas where 60 to 80
percent of renters are cost burdened. The rates of cost burden among renters in Dos Palos is similar
to the region, where 44 percent of renter households experience cost burden.
Approximately 30 percent of total households in Dos Palos are cost burdened and 10 percent of
households are severely cost burdened (Table C5-4). A higher percentage of renter-occupied
households are cost burdened, while a higher percentage of owner-occupied households are

severely cost burdened. Extremely low-, very low-, and low-income renter households experienced
cost burden at disproportionately high rates compared to moderate- and above moderate-income
renter households. Owner-occupied households have higher rates of cost burden for extremely low-
and very low-income households. However, rates of cost burden in moderate- and above moderate-
income owner households are higher than low-income owner households. Overall, cost burden
decreased as incomes increased. Approximately 91 percent of all extremely low-income households

Overcrowding
As discussed in Chapter C3, Housing Needs Assessment, Dos Palos has 355 large households
(households with five or more people), comprising approximately 21 percent of total households, as
shown in Table C5-5. This is one percent lower than the county (22 percent) and two percent higher
than the Northern SJV region average (19 percent). A higher percentage of renter households (12
percent) are large households compared to owner households (nine percent).
Approximately 10 percent of households in Dos Palos are overcrowded, which is greater than the
statewide average of eight percent, and the countywide average of nine percent. The rate of
overcrowded households is higher in East Dos Palos, with approximately 13 percent of all
households being overcrowded. The rate of overcrowding in North and South Dos Palos is much
lower at three percent (Figure C5-23). Overcrowding rates are higher in Dos Palos than the majority
of the county, where overcrowding typically ranges between five and 10 percent. However, the
community of Winton includes areas where overcrowding ranges from 15 to 20 percent, and the
city of Merced contains areas where over 20 percent of households are overcrowded.

Homelessness
According to the 2022 Merced City and County Continuum of Care Point-In-Time (PIT) Count, 855
unhoused individuals were recorded in Merced County and its jurisdictions, representing a two
percent increase since 2021. In Dos Palos, 11 unsheltered and zero unhoused individuals were
recorded in 2022, a decrease of 15 persons from 26 recorded in 2021 (57 percent decrease). 6 The
total population in Dos Palos comprises approximately two percent of the population in Merced
County, and the unhoused population in Dos Palos represents approximately one percent of the
total homeless population recorded in Merced County. As a result, Dos Palos has a roughly
proportional share of the county’s unhoused population.
The PIT Count does not provide demographic information of the unhoused population for Dos Palos.
According to City staff, concentrations of unhoused residents have been observed along Blossom
Street and the intersections of Central Avenue and Blossom Street and Central Avenue and
Marguerite Street. As referenced in Chapter 5, Regional Assessment of Fair Housing, the majority of
the unhoused population in Merced County are white (67 percent).
The Rock Church and Sacred Heart Catholic Church help provide services to unhoused individuals.
The City usually contacts the County and Continuum of Care staff to help guide people through the
process. Figure C5-24 shows the locations of the churches, City Hall, and the hospitals in Dos Palos.
These services are in relatively close proximity to each other.
Based on observations by City staff who have lived in Dos Palos most of their lives, many unhoused
individuals within the city are originally from Dos Palos, and do not want to stay with their friends
and/or families. According to Police Department, when asked if they would like to go home, many of
them refuse and would rather continue living in the streets. While obtaining funding for programs
that for the unhoused population is a challenge, the refusal of the local unhoused population to
actually go home to their friends/families has proven to be a challenge in itself.

Displacement
The Urban Displacement Project (UDP) designates communities as at risk of displacement if the
share of very low-income residents is greater than 20 percent and have any of the two following
characteristics:
   The share of renters is above 40 percent
   The share of people of color is above 50 percent
   The share of very low-income households that are severely rent burdened is above the county
    median
   The percent change in rent is above the county median for rent increases

According to the UDP, the entire city is considered to have a low risk of displacement (Figure C5-25).
Home values and rents have increased significantly in Dos Palos over the past decade. Between
2015 and 2021, median home value increased from $96,300 to $252,800 (163 percent increase) and
median rent increased from $783 to $1,042 (33 percent increase). In addition, about 30 percent of
all households are cost burdened, meaning many households are paying too much for housing.

C5.11 Local Area Knowledge
Historic Patterns of Segregation
Founded in the 1890s, Dos Palos began as a colony developed by former school principal Bernhard
Marks through the purchasing of land by the Miller and Lux Company, which owned much of the
land on the west side of Merced County. Marks brought forty pioneer families west, mostly from
Iowa and Nebraska, to establish the community. In 1892, unable to find good water, many of the
settlers left. Marks convinced Miller to establish another town two miles away on land unsuitable
for farming and ranching due to swamps, and unsettling soils. Some of the settlers relocated. This
new town was named Colony Center, California. In 1906, Dos Palos Colony was renamed South Dos
Palos and Colony Center was renamed Dos Palos. About a dozen of the colony’s original families still
reside locally.
Land reclamation was needed to properly drain land north of Dos Palos to prepare it for intensive
agriculture. Ditches, levees, and canals were dug to provide irrigation across the colony. Due to
these efforts, large acreages of cotton, grain, flax, alfalfa, and beans were possible. Dairy also
became a prominent industry in the city.
Through the years, people from many other locations joined the community including Italians in the
1910s, Azoreans in the 1920s, Japanese in the 1930s, Army Air Corps Cadets from across the nation
to train at Eagle Field in the 1940s, white and black dust bowl migrants from Oklahoma, Texas, and
Arkansas in the 1950s to work the cotton fields, and in the 21 st century, a strong infusion of Mexican
and Asian cultures. Consistent with the city’s history influx of diverse racial/ethnic groups, new
developments are generally occupied by a mix of racial/ethnic residents. However, housing
development in the city has remained stagnant since approximately 2010 due to the lack of water.
The lack of water availability is the city’s biggest challenge to developing more housing.
Aside from challenges with water availability, the City is experiencing other challenges in providing
various housing due to issues with older public infrastructure. In many instances, sewer lines are
clogging up, causing backflow issues in certain parts of the city on a regular basis. Water lines are
also consistently failing in areas and staff are conducting temporary repairs as a band-aid in lieu of
replacing the old, aging systems. These older infrastructure facilities are generally located in the
northeast quadrant of the city in the neighborhoods around Dora Street and Lorraine Street. The
City was able to replace public facilities on Lorraine Street around 2019, when Center Street was
resurfaced. However, the City has not been able to replace lines within the neighborhood due to
lack of funding. These lines are generally made of clay and would need to be upgraded. The City
intends to replace those lines when funding becomes available and are prioritized via a list of streets
the City intends to either repair or resurface.
Due to an old General Plan (adopted in the 1990s), the City potentially lacks the ability to annex new
land because the goals and policies of that plan are inconsistent with the findings necessary for the
Local Agency Formation Commission of Merced County to approve any annexations. Therefore, any
new housing projects would have to occur within the City’s current limits where the city has limited
stock of land or property to develop. This poses another challenge for developing affordable
projects.

Stakeholder and Community Input
   A community workshop was held in Dos Palos on August 30, 2023. During the workshop,
    participants expressed that they hope to see an increase in homeownership for all levels of
    income, race, and age. In addition, participants cited that a lack of available housing and
    affordable housing, particularly for farmworkers, makes it difficult to find housing. Almost all
    farmworkers are cost burdened.
   Homeownership is very difficult.
   There is a lack of housing with supportive services, particularly for residents with mental health
    disabilities.
   Lack of public transportation options makes it difficult for people to find housing that meets
    their needs. Additionally, there is limited access to commercial services, which means that
    people must drive to other cities.
   Residents desire rent control.
   Historic pattern of racial segregation in Dos Palos has segregated neighborhoods.
   Housing rehabilitation and repair was the most voted programs to address housing needs with
    nine votes. This was followed by rent-restricted affordable housing development and housing
    for special needs populations, which both received eight votes. Renter protections and support
    received six votes. One participant commented that renter protection is needed, as there are
    not enough attorneys for renters.
   Many seniors are on Social Security and are severely cost burdened and homes are not ADA
    accessible.

The City also participated in a series of stakeholder interviews with service providers, community
organizations, and affordable and market-rate housing developers held between August 8 and
August 23, 2023. Community organizations identified the need for housing near medical facilities
and public transportation. Additional housing needs include transitional housing and citywide and
countywide rent control. Compared to larger cities in the region, smaller, rural areas have vastly
fewer amenities and housing resources. According to market-rate housing developers, barriers to
developing housing include high construction costs, limited resources offered for affordable housing
within the central coast, and lack of subsidies for affordable housing units. Affordable housing
developers described the need for more attainable zoning and entitlement approvals and the
necessity of transit being near affordable housing locations. According to affordable housing
developers, cities can foster strong relationships with affordable housing providers and maintain
knowledgeable staff to pursue grant opportunities for affordable housing.
An online community survey was available on the Merced County Association of Governments
Housing Element website in both English and Spanish from May to December 2023. The survey
asked participants about housing issues and the types and location of housing development they
would like to see in their city. Respondents in Dos Palos identified the availability of desirable
housing and affordability of desired housing as the most urgent housing challenges. According to
respondents in Dos Palos, the largest barriers to affording desirable housing in the city are the high
costs of quality housing and the lack of housing. Housing needs identified by respondents in Dos
Palos housing with three or more bedrooms. When asked about their preferences for the location of
future housing development, respondents said they would like to see housing in areas near public
transit stops, employment, and shopping centers.

C5.11.1 Local Setting
Dos Palos was part of the “Rancho Sanjon de Santa Rita” Mexican Land Grant, which cites “Los Dos
Palos” or “The Two Trees” as a boundary marker. In 1891, former school principal Bernhard Marks
convinced “Cattle King” Henry Miller to develop a small town nearby In 1892, unable to find good
water, many of the settlers left. Marks convinced Miller to establish another town two miles away
on land unsuitable for farming and ranching due to swamps, and unsettling soils. Some of the
settlers relocated. This new town was named Colony Center, California. In 1906, Dos Palos Colony
was renamed South Dos Palos and Colony Center was renamed Dos Palos.
Suburban and residential development in Dos Palos has been modest compared to larger cities but
has gradually expanded over time. Initially, the town’s growth was driven primarily by its agricultural
roots, with housing centered around farmworkers and local businesses. As the population
increased, particularly after World War II, Dos Palos began to see more suburban-style residential
neighborhoods emerge to accommodate a growing workforce. The town’s development has been
influenced by its proximity to larger cities in the Central Valley, offering a more affordable and
quieter alternative for families seeking to escape the urban sprawl. Newer housing developments
have been built in recent decades, providing modern amenities while maintaining the town’s small-
town character.

Land Uses and Development Trends
Dos Palos has traditionally been a residential community, which has impacted the way the city has
developed over the years. Over 60 percent of the land in the city is designated for residential uses.
Of the total housing units, 94 percent are single-family homes. As described above, the majority of
residences are located in the North, East, and South Dos Palos. Figure C5-26 shows the City’s Zoning
Map and shows the residential, agricultural, commercial and industrial areas of the city. Despite the
prevalence of single-family housing in Dos Palos, almost 39 percent of households are renters. As
illustrated in Figure C5-27, renter units are concentrated in East Dos Palos. Although a higher
concentration of renters is also shown in West Dos Palos, this reflects the unincorporated areas as
there are few housing units within city boundaries.
Figure C5-28 illustrates Dos Palos’ suburban and agricultural development. The city is primarily
surrounded by agricultural land in the unincorporated county. North Dos Palos is mostly residential
uses, while residential, commercial and manufacturing uses are in East and South Dos Palos. West
Dos Palos has very little housing and is zoned for manufacturing uses. The largest proportion of
multifamily housing units are located in East Dos Palos.
As a result of these development patterns and land use zoning, a greater percentage of the
population lives in North and South Dos Palos (Census Tract 24.04) between Reynolds and Center
Avenues (Figure C5-29). Figure C5-30 also shows historical development patterns, with older
housing primarily located in East Dos Palos.

C5.11.2 Other Relevant Factors
Other factors to fair housing issues in Dos Palos that have not been previously discussed in this
analysis include language barriers and lack of farmworker housing. These factors limit the
accumulation of wealth and access to housing resources in historically marginalized communities.

Limited English Proficiency
Language barriers can lead to linguistic and cultural isolation. According to the 2017-2021 ACS, 51
percent of residents within Dos Palos speak a language other than English at home, and the majority
of those speak Spanish.

Farmworker Housing Needs
Much of the land surrounding Dos Palos is utilized for agricultural operations and approximately 21
percent of Dos Palos’ population (488 persons) works in agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting,
and mining. Dos Palos is located near the jurisdictions of Los Banos, Firebaugh, and Chowchilla, all of
which contain expansive agricultural operations in the vicinity of Dos Palos. Farmworkers employed
by nearby agricultural businesses may seek housing in Dos Palos. However, the migratory and often
seasonal nature of farm work often makes it difficult for farmworkers to find affordable housing
options. There is currently no public or subsidized housing for farmworkers in Dos Palos. The
Housing Authority of the County of Merced (HACM) operates one property for farmworkers in the
community of Planada approximately 36miles from Dos Palos. HACM also operates several migrant
housing centers across Merced County. No farmworker housing is located within Dos Palos city
limits.

Housing Stock Type
The vast majority of the housing stock (84 percent) is made up of detached single-family homes,
which may not be affordable to lower-income households.
Dos Palos has 335 large households (households with five or more people), or approximately 21
percent of total households. A higher percentage of renter households (31 percent) are considered
large households compared to owner households (15 percent). Only 13 percent of all housing units
contain four or more bedrooms. These larger units can typically accommodate large families
without overcrowding.

C5.11.3 Conclusion
Historical land use and zoning practices in Dos Palos have impacted housing choices and mobility,
particularly for lLow- and mModerate-iIncome (LMI)LMI residents and communities of color. Several
factors, including restrictive zoning, and disparities in investment, have contributed to these
outcomes.

Development history
Dos Palos, initially centered on agriculture, saw modest suburban expansion after World War II, with
94 percent of its housing stock made up of single-family homes. While this pattern reflects a focus
on homeownership, it has not necessarily made homeownership more accessible today. During a
community workshop in 2023, participants expressed that the lack of affordable housing options,—
especially for farmworkers and LMI residents, —makes homeownership very difficult. The


C5-54
                                                                                        City of Dos Palos
                                                            Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing (AFFH)

predominance of single-family homes, combined with high construction costs and limited new
affordable housing developments, has contributed to a shortage of available, affordable housing.
Even neighborhoods with older, lower-value homes like East Dos Palos still remain out of reach for
many potential homeowners, particularly residents who face additional economic challenges such
as those on fixed incomes or farmworkers.

Restrictive Zoning
The City’s zoning is predominantly residential, with about 60 percent of land designated for housing,
mostly for single-family units. Multi-family housing, however, is concentrated primarily in East Dos
Palos, where there is also a higher concentration of poverty and segregation. This zoning pattern
limits the availability of diverse housing types, such as affordable multi-family units, elsewhere in
the city, which may have contributed to a lack of affordable housing options and limited mobility for
LMI households. While zoning practices have not been explicitly exclusionary, they likely reflect
broader structural trends seen across many U.S. cities, where single-family zoning can limit access to
more affordable housing options.
The reliance on single-family housing and the lack of affordable housing options in Dos Palos restrict
mobility, particularly for renters, who make up about 39 percent of the city’s population. Renters in
areas like East Dos Palos face higher rates of housing cost burden, with many spending more than
30% of their income on housing. This dynamic may limit economic mobility and opportunities for
these residents, though the city’s overall risk of displacement is low.
Stakeholder interviews with affordable housing developers, conducted between August 8 and 23,
2023, further highlighted the need for more flexible zoning and streamlined entitlement approvals
to facilitate affordable housing projects. Developers also pointed to the need for affordable housing
near transit hubs, which is currently lacking in Dos Palos.

Disparities in Investment
There are notable differences in investment and development across different parts of Dos Palos.
North and South Dos Palos, which have higher incomes and a higher concentration of non-white
residents, have seen more recent development and infrastructure improvements. In contrast, areas
like East Dos Palos have older infrastructure and have experienced fewer upgrades, and have aging
sewer and water lines that continue to require temporary repairs. These disparities in infrastructure
and public investment likely contribute to ongoing economic inequality and may have limited the
overall development potential of these neighborhoods.
Participants in the August 30, 2023 workshop identified housing rehabilitation and repair as the
most important programs to address housing needs, followed by the development of rent-restricted
affordable housing and housing for special needs populations. The lack of public transportation
further exacerbates mobility challenges, as residents must often travel to nearby cities for
commercial services.

C5.12 Subsidized Housing
According to the California Housing Partnership, there are no affordable housing buildings in Dos
Palos, but there is one affordable housing building just outside the City’s boundaries located east of
State Route 33, south of Valeria Street and west of Carol Avenue. The Dos Palos Apartments
complex, built in 1989, contains 78 affordable units.

C5.13 Housing Site Inventory Analysis
This portion of the AFFH analyzes the relation between the housing opportunity sites and AFFH-
related issues. Government Code Section 65583(c)(10) requires the housing opportunity sites to be
analyzed with respect to AFFH to ensure that sites designated for low-income households are
dispersed equitably throughout the city rather than concentrated in areas of high segregation and
poverty or low-resource areas that have historically been underserved, and conversely, that sites
designated for above moderate-income households are not concentrated in areas of high resources.
By comparing the sites inventory to the fair housing indicators in this assessment, this section
analyzes whether the sites included in the Housing Element Site Inventory improve or exacerbate
fair housing conditions, patterns of segregation, and access to opportunity.
The City’s Site Inventory can accommodate 479 housing units on 17 sites plus an additional 162
units in the pipeline project for a total of 641 units (235 lower income, 116 moderate income, and
290 above moderate income).

Housing Sites by TCAC Opportunity Area
For purposes of evaluating fair housing, resource levels designated by TCAC/HCD denote access to
economic and educational opportunities such as low-cost transportation, jobs, and high-quality
schools and the quality of environmental factors in the area such as proximity to hazards and air
quality. TCAC has a composite opportunity score for each census tract. The majority of the city is
designated as a “moderate-resource” area. West Dos Palos is designated as a “low-resource” area,
as is the area west of Lexington Avenue outside city limits. The City does not have any areas
considered “high resource.” Figure C5-32 shows the location of the Housing Element opportunity
sites by TCAC-designated resource area. All of the housing opportunity sites as well as the pipeline
project (Elrod Subdivision, “P” in map) are located in moderate-resource areas.
Figure C5-32 shows the housing opportunity sites by TCAC designated resource area. The housing
opportunity sites are designated by income category – whether the sites could accommodate
housing appropriate for low-, moderate-, or above moderate-income households. The
“appropriateness” of sites for various affordability levels is dictated by State housing element law
and HCD guidance and includes allowable density, size of site, realistic capacity, existing use(s), and
other factors. More information about the sites and income designations is available in Appendix E,
Housing Resources.

where overcrowding is prevalent, the Site Inventory will add new housing opportunities in areas
that need them.

According to the UDP, new market-rate construction in gentrifying areas neither worsens nor eases

subsidized housing construction and housing preservation to help existing residents stay in their
neighborhood. The mix of lower-, moderate, and above moderate-income housing units in North
Dos Palos and, East Dos Palos, and the Midway Annexation will provide affordable housing options
for existing lower-income residents as well as encourage higher-income households to move into
the area. The Site Inventory will add new rental housing opportunities which may alleviate high
costs due to lack of availability.

C5.14 Contributing Factors and Meaningful Actions
AB 686 requires an identification and prioritization of contributing factors to fair housing issues
based on all the previously required analysis (outreach, fair housing assessment, site inventory). This
section lists contributing factors that create, perpetuate, or increase the severity of one or more fair
housing issues identified in community outreach and the analysis in this document. Contributing
factors were prioritized based on their impact on fair housing issues as well as the City’s ability to
address the contributing factors. Chapter C7, Housing Plan, includes a summary of the identified fair
housing issues, contributing factors to these issues, and meaningful actions the city will undertake
to affirmatively further fair housing for special needs, racial/ethnic minorities, and low-income
residents.

Enforcement and Outreach
The City’s website has no information on fair housing, fair housing rights and responsibilities for
tenants and landlords. In addition, there is no housing information on the City’s website.
Contributing factors to fair housing enforcement and outreach in Dos Palos include:
   Language Barriers (Medium): Fifty-one percent of the population of Dos Palos speaks a language
    other than English. Information on the city’s website is provided only in English.
   Lack of local public or private fair housing outreach and enforcement (High): The city does not
    provide its own fair housing outreach or enforcement and does not provide information on
    partnering agencies or fair housing organizations to provide assistance to tenants and landlords.
   Lack of resources for fair housing agencies and organizations on the city’s website. (High)
   Lack of local fair housing laws to support strong enforcement. (Low)
   Lack of sufficient distribution of fair housing information: The city’s website does not provide
    housing information on the city’s website. (High)
   Lack of fair housing testing. (Medium)
   Limited participation in fair housing outreach. (Medium)
   Rationale: Resources to educate, investigate, and enforce fair housing complaints are key to
    ensuring fair housing protections are accessible and effective for protected classes. In addition,
    proactive interventions to fair housing issues prevent displacement.

Segregation and Integration Patterns and Trends
Dos Palos is predominantly Hispanic/Latino with a high rate of poverty, a high percentage of low-
and moderate-incomeLMI residents, and low median household incomes. In particular, East Dos
Palos has a higher of residents with a disability and female single-parent households. South Dos
Palos has a higher percentage of non-white residents. Multi-family residential zones are typically
concentrated in East Dos Palos.
Contributing factors to segregation and integration patterns and trends in Dos Palos include:
   Location and type of affordable housing (High): No affordable housing is located within the city’s
    boundaries.
   Displacement of residents due to economic pressures (Medium): Home values and rents have
    increased significantly in Dos Palos over the past decade. Between 2015 and 2021, home value
    increased from $96,300 to $252,800 (163 percent increase) and median rent increased from
    $783 to $1,042 (33 percent increase) (2011-2015 and 2017-2021 ACS). In addition, about 30


2024-2032 Housing Element                                                                          C5-77
Merced County Association of Governments
Merced County Multi-Jurisdictional Housing Element (2024-2032)

    percent of all households are cost burdened, meaning many households are paying too much
    for housing. While the UDP rates the City as a low risk of displacement, these trends indicate
    cost burdened and low-income households may be at risk of displacement if the cost of housing
    continues to rise.
   Lack of community revitalization strategies (Medium)
   Lack of private investments in specific neighborhoods (High)
   Lack of public investments in specific neighborhoods, including services or amenities (Medium)
   Rationale: Efforts to deconcentrate segregation should focus on two key areas: increasing
    affordable housing in both high-poverty and low-poverty neighborhoods to facilitate mobility
    and implementing measures to incentivize affordable housing development and expand
    opportunities in areas with higher resources.

Racially and Ethnically Concentrated Areas of Poverty
There are no areas of high segregation and poverty, but East Dos Palos has a high percent of LMI
residents, low median income, and a non-white population of 59 percent. This census tract also has
the highest percentage of residents living with a disability and percentage of female single-parent
households.
Contributing factors to racially and ethnically concentrated areas of poverty in Dos Palos include:
   Displacement of residents due to economic pressures (Medium): High rates of cost burden and
    rising housing costs are placing low-income residents at risk of displacement.
   Land use and zoning laws (Medium): Most of Dos Palos is zoned for single-family residential uses
    with medium- and high-density residential zoning concentrated in East Dos Palos.
   Location and type of affordable housing (High): There are no affordable housing units within Dos
    Palos.
   Rationale: Efforts to deconcentrate areas with a concentration of minorities and poverty should
    focus on two key areas: increasing affordable housing in both high-poverty and low-poverty
    neighborhoods to facilitate mobility and implementing measures to incentivize affordable
    housing development and expand opportunities in areas with higher resources.

Disproportionate Housing Needs
Cost burden among renters is high throughout the city, and is highest in East Dos Palos. Cost burden
among homeowners high throughout the city. Dos Palos has a high percentage of large households,
approximately 21 percent of all households in the city. Overcrowding is highest in East Dos Palos.
This area has the lowest household median incomes, indicating that residents may not be able
afford to afford to pay for repair and maintenance on their homes.
Contributing factors to disproportionate housing needs in Dos Palos include:
   Prevalence of cost burden (High): Home values and rent has increased significantly in Dos Palos
    over the past decade, which causes increased cost burden among homeowners and renters.
    According to 2015-2019 CHAS data, approximately 30 percent of all households in Dos Palos are
    cost burdened.
   Lack of affordable housing in a range of sizes (High): The vast majority of the housing stock (84
    percent) is made up of detached single-family homes, which may not be affordable to lower-
    income households. Only 13 percent of all housing units contain four or more bedrooms which
    can accommodate large families without overcrowding.


C5-78
                                                                                         City of Dos Palos
                                                             Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing (AFFH)

   Cost of housing maintenance and repairs (Medium): Dos Palos’ older housing stock indicates
    that a significant number of housing units are in need of repair.
   Rationale: The lack of affordable housing options can restrict individuals and families to a
    limited number of choices, forcing them to settle for substandard housing or pay a
    disproportionate amount of their income on rent. This can perpetuate cycles of poverty and
    limit upward mobility.

Disparities in Access to Opportunities
Most of Dos Palos is considered moderate-resource. However, the entire city has a high pollution
burden, low economic opportunity, and is designated as a disadvantaged community.
Contributing factors to disparities in access to opportunities in Dos Palos include:
The availability, type, frequency, and reliability of public transportation: There is only one public
transit on-demand option in the city, which serves the entire west side of Merced County.
 Lack of walkability (Medium): North and South Dos Palos are the most walkable, while other
    areas of the city have below average walkability.
 Land use and zoning patterns (High): The zones that permit multi-family housing within the city
    are concentrated in East Dos Palos. The remainder of the city is low density single-family
    housing, which limits the amount of multi-family housing that can be built throughout the city.
 High pollution burden (Medium): All of Dos Palos is ranked in the 80 th percentile for pollution
    burden by CalEnviroScreen.
 Lack of public and private investment (High): Without investment, businesses are less likely to
    locate in these areas, leading to a lack of jobs and economic growth. This can create a cycle of
    poverty, as residents struggle to find employment and generate income.
 Rationale: Improving economic opportunities requires a range of policies designed to create
    jobs, develop the workforce, create housing closer to jobs and ensure that workers can get to
    jobs. More jobs and more affordable housing give residents more housing choices (type of
    housing and mobility).

C5.15 Meaningful Actions to Address Fair Housing Issues
The findings of this analysis were used to develop meaningful actions, metrics and milestones that
promote inclusive communities, increase housing opportunities, and address racial/ethnic and
economic disparities in the city. The contributing factors were prioritized to better formulate
policies and programs and carry out meaningful actions to further fair housing. Meaningful actions
to address fair housing issues are included in the housing programs located in Chapter C7, Housing
Plan.

C6.2 Meeting the RHNA
Each jurisdic on must iden fy adequate land with appropriate zoning and development standards
to fulﬁll its share of the RHNA. Jurisdic ons can use planned and/or approved projects, es mated
accessory dwelling unit (ADU) produc on, and vacant and/or underu lized sites to accommodate
the RHNA. In some cases, rezoning must occur to ready sites for future residen al development.
Once the City has demonstrated in the Housing Element that it has the development capacity to
accommodate the RHNA, it has two implementa on-related obliga ons during the planning period:
1. Maintain a “no net loss” policy of its residen al development capacity over the housing element
   planning period, meaning that sites listed in the adopted Housing Element land inventory may
   not be down-zoned to a lower-density residen al zone or rezoned to a nonresiden al zone,
   unless the City up-zones or rezones alterna ve sites prior to the density reduc on or rezone on
   the inventoried site.
2. Con nue to allocate available funding resources to and facilitate the development of aﬀordable
   housing.

C6.3 Methodology
C6.3.1 Suitable Sites for Affordable Housing
State law requires that jurisdic ons demonstrate in the Housing Element that the land inventory is
adequate to accommodate that jurisdic on’s share of the regional growth. State law has established
“default” density standards for the purpose of es ma ng poten al units by income range. In a
suburban jurisdic on, a density standard of 20 or more units per acre (primarily for higher density
mul -family developments) would facilitate the development of housing in the lower-income
category.

In addi on to default density standards, the California Legislature established size requirements for
parcels intended to support the development of lower-income units. Government Code Sec on
65583.2 establishes that sites between 0.5 and 10 acres in size which are zoned for residen al
development at greater than 20 units per acre are suitable for lower-income projects. Very small
parcels, even when zoned for high densi es, may not facilitate the scale of development required to
access compe ve funding resources. Conversely, typically lower-resource aﬀordable housing
developers may be unable to ﬁnance the scale of project necessitated by very large parcels. No
standalone parcels smaller than 0.5 acres are assumed to accommodate lower-income units. The
City assumed no more than 150 lower-income units on any individual site.

Nonvacant sites included on the Site Inventory have comparable predevelopment characteris cs to
developed residen al projects in the region. As discussed in Chapter 4, Regional Development
Trends, residen al development in Merced County has occurred primarily on vacant sites and sites
occupied by agriculture.
