C5.14 Contributing Factors and Meaningful Actions
AB 686 requires an identification and prioritization of contributing factors to fair housing issues
based on all the previously required analysis (outreach, fair housing assessment, site inventory). This
section lists contributing factors that create, perpetuate, or increase the severity of one or more fair
housing issues identified in community outreach and the analysis in this document. Contributing
factors were prioritized based on their impact on fair housing issues as well as the City’s ability to
address the contributing factors. Chapter C7, Housing Plan, includes a summary of the identified fair
housing issues, contributing factors to these issues, and meaningful actions the city will undertake
to affirmatively further fair housing for special needs, racial/ethnic minorities, and low-income
residents.

Enforcement and Outreach
The City’s website has no information on fair housing, fair housing rights and responsibilities for
tenants and landlords. In addition, there is no housing information on the City’s website.
Contributing factors to fair housing enforcement and outreach in Dos Palos include:
   Language Barriers (Medium): Fifty-one percent of the population of Dos Palos speaks a language
    other than English. Information on the city’s website is provided only in English.
   Lack of local public or private fair housing outreach and enforcement (High): The city does not
    provide its own fair housing outreach or enforcement and does not provide information on
    partnering agencies or fair housing organizations to provide assistance to tenants and landlords.
   Lack of resources for fair housing agencies and organizations on the city’s website. (High)
   Lack of local fair housing laws to support strong enforcement. (Low)
   Lack of sufficient distribution of fair housing information: The city’s website does not provide
    housing information on the city’s website. (High)
   Lack of fair housing testing. (Medium)
   Limited participation in fair housing outreach. (Medium)
   Rationale: Resources to educate, investigate, and enforce fair housing complaints are key to
    ensuring fair housing protections are accessible and effective for protected classes. In addition,
    proactive interventions to fair housing issues prevent displacement.

Segregation and Integration Patterns and Trends
Dos Palos is predominantly Hispanic/Latino with a high rate of poverty, a high percentage of low-
and moderate-incomeLMI residents, and low median household incomes. In particular, East Dos
Palos has a higher of residents with a disability and female single-parent households. South Dos
Palos has a higher percentage of non-white residents. Multi-family residential zones are typically
concentrated in East Dos Palos.
Contributing factors to segregation and integration patterns and trends in Dos Palos include:
   Location and type of affordable housing (High): No affordable housing is located within the city’s
    boundaries.
   Displacement of residents due to economic pressures (Medium): Home values and rents have
    increased significantly in Dos Palos over the past decade. Between 2015 and 2021, home value
    increased from $96,300 to $252,800 (163 percent increase) and median rent increased from
    $783 to $1,042 (33 percent increase) (2011-2015 and 2017-2021 ACS). In addition, about 30


2024-2032 Housing Element                                                                          C5-77
Merced County Association of Governments
Merced County Multi-Jurisdictional Housing Element (2024-2032)

    percent of all households are cost burdened, meaning many households are paying too much
    for housing. While the UDP rates the City as a low risk of displacement, these trends indicate
    cost burdened and low-income households may be at risk of displacement if the cost of housing
    continues to rise.
   Lack of community revitalization strategies (Medium)
   Lack of private investments in specific neighborhoods (High)
   Lack of public investments in specific neighborhoods, including services or amenities (Medium)
   Rationale: Efforts to deconcentrate segregation should focus on two key areas: increasing
    affordable housing in both high-poverty and low-poverty neighborhoods to facilitate mobility
    and implementing measures to incentivize affordable housing development and expand
    opportunities in areas with higher resources.

Racially and Ethnically Concentrated Areas of Poverty
There are no areas of high segregation and poverty, but East Dos Palos has a high percent of LMI
residents, low median income, and a non-white population of 59 percent. This census tract also has
the highest percentage of residents living with a disability and percentage of female single-parent
households.
Contributing factors to racially and ethnically concentrated areas of poverty in Dos Palos include:
   Displacement of residents due to economic pressures (Medium): High rates of cost burden and
    rising housing costs are placing low-income residents at risk of displacement.
   Land use and zoning laws (Medium): Most of Dos Palos is zoned for single-family residential uses
    with medium- and high-density residential zoning concentrated in East Dos Palos.
   Location and type of affordable housing (High): There are no affordable housing units within Dos
    Palos.
   Rationale: Efforts to deconcentrate areas with a concentration of minorities and poverty should
    focus on two key areas: increasing affordable housing in both high-poverty and low-poverty
    neighborhoods to facilitate mobility and implementing measures to incentivize affordable
    housing development and expand opportunities in areas with higher resources.

Disproportionate Housing Needs
Cost burden among renters is high throughout the city, and is highest in East Dos Palos. Cost burden
among homeowners high throughout the city. Dos Palos has a high percentage of large households,
approximately 21 percent of all households in the city. Overcrowding is highest in East Dos Palos.
This area has the lowest household median incomes, indicating that residents may not be able
afford to afford to pay for repair and maintenance on their homes.
Contributing factors to disproportionate housing needs in Dos Palos include:
   Prevalence of cost burden (High): Home values and rent has increased significantly in Dos Palos
    over the past decade, which causes increased cost burden among homeowners and renters.
    According to 2015-2019 CHAS data, approximately 30 percent of all households in Dos Palos are
    cost burdened.
   Lack of affordable housing in a range of sizes (High): The vast majority of the housing stock (84
    percent) is made up of detached single-family homes, which may not be affordable to lower-
    income households. Only 13 percent of all housing units contain four or more bedrooms which
    can accommodate large families without overcrowding.


C5-78
                                                                                         City of Dos Palos
                                                             Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing (AFFH)

   Cost of housing maintenance and repairs (Medium): Dos Palos’ older housing stock indicates
    that a significant number of housing units are in need of repair.
   Rationale: The lack of affordable housing options can restrict individuals and families to a
    limited number of choices, forcing them to settle for substandard housing or pay a
    disproportionate amount of their income on rent. This can perpetuate cycles of poverty and
    limit upward mobility.

Disparities in Access to Opportunities
Most of Dos Palos is considered moderate-resource. However, the entire city has a high pollution
burden, low economic opportunity, and is designated as a disadvantaged community.
Contributing factors to disparities in access to opportunities in Dos Palos include:
The availability, type, frequency, and reliability of public transportation: There is only one public
transit on-demand option in the city, which serves the entire west side of Merced County.
 Lack of walkability (Medium): North and South Dos Palos are the most walkable, while other
    areas of the city have below average walkability.
 Land use and zoning patterns (High): The zones that permit multi-family housing within the city
    are concentrated in East Dos Palos. The remainder of the city is low density single-family
    housing, which limits the amount of multi-family housing that can be built throughout the city.
 High pollution burden (Medium): All of Dos Palos is ranked in the 80 th percentile for pollution
    burden by CalEnviroScreen.
 Lack of public and private investment (High): Without investment, businesses are less likely to
    locate in these areas, leading to a lack of jobs and economic growth. This can create a cycle of
    poverty, as residents struggle to find employment and generate income.
 Rationale: Improving economic opportunities requires a range of policies designed to create
    jobs, develop the workforce, create housing closer to jobs and ensure that workers can get to
    jobs. More jobs and more affordable housing give residents more housing choices (type of
    housing and mobility).

C5.15 Meaningful Actions to Address Fair Housing Issues
The findings of this analysis were used to develop meaningful actions, metrics and milestones that
promote inclusive communities, increase housing opportunities, and address racial/ethnic and
economic disparities in the city. The contributing factors were prioritized to better formulate
policies and programs and carry out meaningful actions to further fair housing. Meaningful actions
to address fair housing issues are included in the housing programs located in Chapter C7, Housing
Plan.

C6.2 Meeting the RHNA
Each jurisdic on must iden fy adequate land with appropriate zoning and development standards
to fulﬁll its share of the RHNA. Jurisdic ons can use planned and/or approved projects, es mated
accessory dwelling unit (ADU) produc on, and vacant and/or underu lized sites to accommodate
the RHNA. In some cases, rezoning must occur to ready sites for future residen al development.
Once the City has demonstrated in the Housing Element that it has the development capacity to
accommodate the RHNA, it has two implementa on-related obliga ons during the planning period:
1. Maintain a “no net loss” policy of its residen al development capacity over the housing element
   planning period, meaning that sites listed in the adopted Housing Element land inventory may
   not be down-zoned to a lower-density residen al zone or rezoned to a nonresiden al zone,
   unless the City up-zones or rezones alterna ve sites prior to the density reduc on or rezone on
   the inventoried site.
2. Con nue to allocate available funding resources to and facilitate the development of aﬀordable
   housing.

C6.3 Methodology
C6.3.1 Suitable Sites for Affordable Housing
State law requires that jurisdic ons demonstrate in the Housing Element that the land inventory is
adequate to accommodate that jurisdic on’s share of the regional growth. State law has established
“default” density standards for the purpose of es ma ng poten al units by income range. In a
suburban jurisdic on, a density standard of 20 or more units per acre (primarily for higher density
mul -family developments) would facilitate the development of housing in the lower-income
category.

In addi on to default density standards, the California Legislature established size requirements for
parcels intended to support the development of lower-income units. Government Code Sec on
65583.2 establishes that sites between 0.5 and 10 acres in size which are zoned for residen al
development at greater than 20 units per acre are suitable for lower-income projects. Very small
parcels, even when zoned for high densi es, may not facilitate the scale of development required to
access compe ve funding resources. Conversely, typically lower-resource aﬀordable housing
developers may be unable to ﬁnance the scale of project necessitated by very large parcels. No
standalone parcels smaller than 0.5 acres are assumed to accommodate lower-income units. The
City assumed no more than 150 lower-income units on any individual site.

Nonvacant sites included on the Site Inventory have comparable predevelopment characteris cs to
developed residen al projects in the region. As discussed in Chapter 4, Regional Development
Trends, residen al development in Merced County has occurred primarily on vacant sites and sites
occupied by agriculture.

C6.4.2 Market Demand
Demand for residen al development of formerly agricultural land in the San Joaquin Valley is high,
and driven by the cri cal need for more housing, necessity for less water-intensive land use, and the
declining property values of agricultural lands due to constrained water resources. The Sustainable
Groundwater Management Act (SGMA) has signiﬁcantly impacted agricultural land use throughout
California. Groundwater sustainability plans now require reduc ons in groundwater use, which
could result in the fallowing of between 500,000 and 900,000 acres of cropland in the San Joaquin
Valley. The conversion of agricultural land to urban development, which primarily occurs around
exis ng communi es, results in a much less water intensive use of land than cropland.1 Coun es
throughout the San Joaquin Valley have no ced decreasing property values for agricultural lands in
response to limited water supply.2 Between 2016 and 2018, 74,641 acres of farmland and grazing
lands were converted to other uses in California, including 37,583 acres of land that were urbanized.

Palos city limits has been converted to urban and built-up land, including land in South Dos Palos
where the nonvacant sites are located.6 Trends illustra ng local conversion of farmland to urban

zoning requirements in each jurisdic on. The average density of projects with aﬀordable units is

percent of the maximum density allowed by the zoning district.

C6.5.1 Realistic Development Capacity
To create a realis c development assump on, the City assumes that the development capacity on
each site will be less than the full development capacity allowed by the parcel's zoning or land use
designa on. Sites do not always develop to their full capacity poten al due to factors such as site-
speciﬁc condi ons and development standards such as open space or parking requirements. To
determine a realis c development achievement on the sites in the inventory, the City reviewed
pipeline and recently developed projects in the region, development standards and site-speciﬁc
condi ons. As discussed in Chapter 4, Regional Development Trends, the average achieved density
for projects collec vely in the region is 70 percent. Based on Based on local and regional trends,
trends, the City conserva vely assumes the realis c capacity of each site would be 70 percent of the
maximum allowable density in the R-1-10, R-1-6, and R-2, and the minimum allowable density (20
dwelling units per acre) in the R-3 and MU zones.

C6.5.2 Likelihood of 100 Percent Nonresidential Uses on Sites
The City iden ﬁes 161 389 units in the MU zone, which allows for 100 percent nonresiden al uses.
In accordance with State law, the Housing Element must consider the likelihood of nonresiden al
development on sites that allow for nonresiden al uses. The MU zone is the only zone that allows
100 percent non-residen al development in which sites were selected.
The Site Inventory considers poten al nonresiden al development in these zones by assuming
conserva ve realis c densi es in this zone compared to past and current trends and maintaining an
adequate buﬀer of units for all RHNA income categories. There are no current trends of
development within the MU zone, since the development of the MU zone is happening in
congruence with the 6th cycle Housing Element. Elsewhere in the San Joaquin Valley, residen al uses
occurred on approximately 18 percent of projects in mixed-use zones in the City of Visalia between

C6.6.2 Annexation Sites
Annexa on is the process by which a city adds land to its jurisdic onal boundaries. Following
annexa on, the city extends its services, laws, and vo ng privileges to meet the needs of residents
living in the annexed area. Typically, annexa on takes place in areas that are adjacent to a
municipality, where the popula on already has expanded to densi es found in urban areas.
Annexa on encourages orderly growth and provides standardized services to those who live in the
annexed area. In Dos Palos, the annexa on process is a shared procedure between Merced County
and the City of Dos Palos, overseen by the Local Agency Forma on Commission of Merced County
(LAFCo).
There are currently two sites that are an cipated to be annexed into Dos Palos and made available
for development during the 6th cycle. Three phases of annexa on within the City’s sphere of
inﬂuence are an cipated; these parcels are located within the ﬁrst phase. The City has worked with
the property owners of these sites to commit a por on of the land to residen al zoning with an
assumed 161 total units across these parcels. The City has ini ated the annexa on process with
LAFCo and it is an cipated that these parcels will be annexed to the City and developed with
residen al uses by midAugust- 20265. To ensure these parcels are available for development during
the planning period, the City will con nue to work with property owners and LAFCo to facilitate the
annexa on of these parcels. AllThe annexa ons are an cipated to be completed by the August of
2026.
These sites are currently zoned General Agriculture (A-1) General Commercial (C-2). Zoning across
the annexed parcels will accommodate mixed-use residen al development. These sites can
accommodate units in each income category. Table C6-11 shows the an cipated size and unit
assump ons for each annexa on and Figure C6-2 shows the loca ons of these annexa on sites.

C6.8 Availability of Infrastructure and Services
The City’s Public Works Department is responsible for the City’s water system, wastewater system,
storm drain system, parks system, storm drainage system, street system, landscaped areas,
municipal buildings and City vehicles and heavy equipment. As such, the City will ensure adequate
capacity of all infrastructure and u li es to accommodate the housing growth discussed in this
Housing Element. As it stands today, City infrastructure does not have capacity to support future
residen al development, however, with development of the water plant infrastructure capacity will
be suﬃcient. Within one week of adop on, the City will provide a copy of the adopted 2024-2032
Housing Element to the City’s Public Works Department Division, pursuant to Government Code
Sec on 65589.7.

C6.8.1 Wastewater System
The City’s exis ng sewer system is comprised of sewer lines with diameters between 4 and 15
inches. There are seven li sta ons that help convey the wastewater to the wastewater treatment
facility for processing. The exis ng sewer lines and li sta ons are adequate for ﬂows. The current
average daily ﬂow to the facility is about 500,000 gallons per day (gpd), or 0.5 million gallons per day
(MGD). The maximum capacity of the wastewater treatment facility is 0.77 MGD. Expansion
capacity can be doubled with the addi on of two new large-berm post treatment basins. All post
treatment water is available and used onsite for non-edible agricultural farming. The City an cipates
adequate wastewater capacity to accommodate development on these sites iden ﬁed to support
the City’s RHNA obliga ons.

C6.8.2 Potable Water System
Dos Palos Water provides drinking water service to its residen al, commercial, industrial, and
ins tu onal customers within the city limits. The City’s municipal water system is supplied by the
California Aqueduct and the San Luis Reservoir. Water is delivered to the City by a 20-inch, 17.5-mile
pipeline, and is treated at a plant and operated by the City’s U li es Department. The City is
currently u lizing 60 to 75 percent of its allo ed water capacity from the Aqueduct depending on
the me of year. The lack of water and near capacity of current facili es in the community is
prohibi ng growth. However, the City, along with its Joint Powers Authority partners and the State
of California, is looking to build a new water plant to meet new state standards. This plant should be
opera onal within two to three years and will double the capacity of the plant from four MGD to
eight MGD.

C6.8.3 Storm Water and Drainage
The City of Dos Palos operates the storm drainage system in coordina on with the Dos Palos
Drainage District (DPDD) and the Central California Irriga on District (CCID). The City of Dos Palos,
DPDD, and CCID operate together to provide storm drainage service within the City’s sphere of
inﬂuence. The City pays the Dos Palos Drainage District to operate three area pumps to reduce the
area’s high water table as needed.
The city’s storm drainage system comprises mul ple small networks that drain into a canal that is
owned and operated by the CCID. Many developed areas in the older por ons of the communi es
of Dos Palos, Midway and South Dos Palos do not have a drainage system. As development in these
areas increases, the City will need to expand the storm drainage system to serve these areas. Since
2010, the City has built two new pumping sta ons, added a large collec on basin, and replaced


2024-2032 Housing Element                                                                         C6-23

Merced County Multi-Jurisdictional Housing Element (2024-2032)

single pump sta on with two or three pump sta ons at nine new loca ons. The City’s stormwater
system has suﬃcient capacity to serve new residen al development necessary to accommodate the
City’s RHNA.

C6.8.4 Dry Utilities
Dry u li es are deﬁned as electricity, natural gas, cable, and telephone services. In Dos Palos, each
dry u lity has one provider: Paciﬁc Gas and Electric Company (PG&E) provides natural gas and
electricity services, Xﬁnity provides cable, and Fron er provides phone and internet services. The
City does not an cipate any issues with connec ng future residen al development sites during the
planning period to these u li es.

C6.9 Environmental Considerations
A city’s environmental se ng and characteris cs can greatly aﬀect the feasibility and cost of
developing housing. As noted in Chapter D4, Housing Constraints Analysis, environmental factors in
Dos Palos include poten al impacts from wildﬁre, drought, ﬂood, and the Williamson Act. There are
no known barriers related to shape, access, contamina on, property condi ons, easements,
conserva on easements, overlays and airport or military compa bility that could impact housing
development on iden ﬁed sites in the planning period.

Wildfire
Dos Palos is located in an urbanized area and is not exposed to wildﬁre hazards. While there are no
ﬁre severity zones within the city boundaries, the city is designated as being at increased risk from
wildﬁres. Poten al impacts of a wildﬁre would not preclude development of housing in Dos Palos.

Drought
As for the impacts of a drought, there will be minimal impact on the physical structures of buildings
and facili es across Dos Palos, however there may be less reliability on infrastructure. The poten al
impacts of a drought would not preclude development of housing in Dos Palos.

Flood
Flood hazards are not a constraint to development, as the city is located outside of the 100-year
ﬂoodplain. The poten al impacts of a drought would not preclude development of housing in Dos
Palos.

Williamson Act
Poten al residen al annexa on areas, where agricultural land is more prevalent, do not include
land that has ac ve Williamson Act contracts. The Williamson Act does not preclude development
within this housing cycle. If the City focuses on annexing lands adjacent to the City in the future,
developments on Williamson Act lands or other parcels with agricultural preserva on restric ons
could be avoided.

C6.10 Opportunities for Energy Conservation
Energy conserva on measures such as weatheriza on, solar energy u liza on, and sustainable
building methods can signiﬁcantly reduce housing costs for households. Residents of Dos Palos are
served by PG&E for electricity and natural gas. The City u lizes the various residen al programs
PG&E oﬀers, including:
   Rebates on energy-eﬃcient appliances
   California Alternate Rates for Energy (CARE) Program, which provides assistance for lower-
    income households
   Family Electric Rate Assistance (FERA) Program for larger households

PG&E's Energy Savings Assistance Program provides free weatheriza on services to qualifying low-
income households. Addi onally, the United States (U.S.) Department of Agriculture Rural
Development has a housing repair program, and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program Block Grant can be u lized to improve energy
eﬃciency in homes. These programs aim to increase eﬃciency, reduce energy consump on, and
lower housing costs for residents in Dos Palos. The City will implement Housing Program 12 which
commits the City to con nuing to provide rehabilita on assistance for energy conserva on and
weatheriza on improvements for homeowners.

HCD Comment (05/08/2025)
Progress in Meeting the Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA): While the element was revised
to clarify that permits will not be issued for the Elrod Subdivision project until the new water treatment
plant is operational in spring 2026, the element should still discuss remaining steps, any other known
barriers to development, and likelihood of construction in the planning period. Additionally, the
element states that the City will continue to monitor this projects through Program 2 and identify
alternative sites if necessary, but must amend Program 2 as noted on page C6-3.




Program 2 (Adequate Sites for RHNA): The City included the Program to complete the annexation to
accommodate the RHNA. However, the Program must be modified and commit to discrete steps with
timing for annexation.

Program 12 (Water and Sewer Service): The element was not revised to address this finding. Please see
HCD’s September 30, 2024 review for additional information.

Prior Review: While the Program was included to update the water and sewer master plans, including
conducting outreach in 2027 and preparing a draft plan by the end of 2028, the element should commit
to implementation earlier in the planning period or analyze and address any impact on identified sites.
It must also include specific commitment to implementing infrastructure improvements, discrete
timelines with milestones and efforts to address any other constraints related to infrastructure
capacity.




Program 6 (Zoning Code Amendments): The Program commits to remove subjective findings for PUDs
and “consider” streamlining the permit review process but should also clearly commit to remove
subjective approval findings (e.g., Finding B) and address public hearing requirements in the Site Plan
Review process.
While the element includes many meaningful actions to affirmatively furthering fair housing (AFFH), it
should expand housing mobility actions and improve place-based strategies toward community
revitalization. For example, the element should commit to applying for funding (beyond prioritizing the
capital improvement program) at least every other year toward broader community development issues
such as neighborhood revitalization, parks, safe routes to school, community facilities and pollution
burdens. Examples of housing mobility actions include promoting more housing choices and
affordability in lower-density areas, religious institutional sites, city-owned sites, prioritizing funding
and enhancing accessory dwelling units (ADU), junior accessory dwelling units (JADU) or additional
conversion of existing single-family space, and home sharing strategies.
